From AI to the return of natural wood: Bona reveals what's ahead for floors in 2027

ENGLEWOOD, Colo. — What's next for the floors beneath our feet? Warmer wood tones continue to gain ground and AI is entering the home-care conversation, though not always with the best results. These are among the trends shaping American homes in 2027, according to the second annual Bona Floorcast, released by Bona, a global leader in flooring and floor care for more than 100 years.
Combining new consumer research with insights from Bona's flooring experts, the report explores how changing design preferences, cleaning habits and technology are influencing homeowners' decisions. And while AI is becoming another resource for home-care advice, what's clear is that traditional expertise still leads the way: flooring contractors and professionals are the most trusted source (50%), far ahead of AI tools (12%).

"We've seen flooring trends come and go, but one thing remains constant: homeowners want beautiful floors that stand the test of time," said Zack Clavin, Bona's flooring expert. "As we look ahead to 2027, homeowners are thinking beyond aesthetics, seeking trusted advice and making more informed decisions about how to care for and protect their floors. It's about looking beyond the immediate results and thinking about the long-term value of their floors."

Key highlights from the 2027 Bona Floorcast include:

Wood floors are here to stay: Wood flooring remains a priority for 60% of homeowners, with interest especially strong among Gen Z (82%), up from 69% last year. Looking ahead, Bona experts see warmer, lighter tones gaining ground as gray fades, with White Oak remaining a favorite, Birch and Beech attracting interest, and wide planks and satin finishes continuing to shape flooring design.

AI Is a resource, but doesn't always get it right: AI is becoming a go-to for home-care advice, but the results don't always live up to expectations. Among the 44% of homeowners using AI for home maintenance, 40% say its advice hasn't worked as expected, with 12% reporting damage.

The cost of clean – Quality Still Counts: Rising household product costs are changing how nearly six in 10 homeowners (58%) shop for cleaning products, but the lowest price isn't always the deciding factor. Nearly nine in 10 (89%) would pay more for at least one desirable feature, particularly better cleaning performance (55%) and floor protection (49%).

Restore, don't replace: More than three-quarters of homeowners (76%) would rather restore their existing wood floors than replace them, assuming they're free of major damage. And that preference is growing stronger, with 44% now strongly agreeing, up from 39% last year, reinforcing the appeal of preserving floors rather than starting from scratch.
Healthy Homes Are Top of Mind: Homeowners are paying closer attention to the products used in their homes, with 87% willing to take at least one action based on indoor air quality or health considerations when installing or refinishing floors. That includes researching products more thoroughly (40%), switching cleaning products (38%) or delaying a project (33%). More than eight in 10 (83%) would also ask a flooring professional which products they plan to use.

"Homeowners want cleaning products that make life easier without sacrificing results," said Stacey Gustafson, Bona cleaning and flooring expert. "It's no surprise that 41% of those changing their shopping habits are looking for products that work across multiple surfaces. The key is finding a cleaner that's right for your floors, so you can simplify your routine without compromising on proper care."

To view the full Floorcast including more insights from Bona's flooring and cleaning experts and additional trends and data, click here. For more information on Bona cleaning tools and solutions for wood floors and other hard surfaces, visit Bona.com.

Survey methodology
The 2027 Bona Floorcast findings are based on a survey conducted by Opinium among 1,000 American homeowners with at least one room featuring wood flooring. Fieldwork was conducted October 15–21, 2026.
